title: Digging a Ditch, Finding a 1,300-Year-Old Treasure!
summary:
Have you ever dug a hole and found something amazing? In Thailand, workers were just digging a drainage ditch near a huge reclining Buddha statue when—clink!—they hit a ceramic container buried over four feet deep. Inside, they found 33 sparkling ornaments made of gold, silver, and bronze. It was like a real-life treasure chest!

The statue is at Wat Thammachak Sema Ram temple. It’s the country’s longest and oldest reclining Buddha: 43 feet long and made way back in 657 A.D. The treasures are from the Dvaravati period, about 1,300 years ago. They include gold rings, silver earrings, and special bronze hoop earrings that match others found across Thailand.

But wait, there’s more! After the first find, the crew kept digging and uncovered three more amazing objects. These were hammered metal sheets with detailed artwork. One is a tiny gold rectangle, about the size of a credit card, showing a seated Buddha with spiral curls, a big halo, and long earlobes. There’s a small hole in the corner, so it was probably hung on a string as decoration or even worn as jewelry.

Another sheet, made of a lead-tin mix, shows a standing Buddha under an arch with two attendants. One attendant might be the Hindu god Brahma! The third piece is a stack of metal sheets crammed in clay, but it’s too damaged to see clearly. Experts think these were ritual offerings placed behind the Buddha’s head on purpose.

Phanombutr Chantrachot, the director-general of Thailand’s Fine Arts Department, said the discovery helps us understand ancient art and beliefs. So next time you’re digging in your backyard, keep your eyes peeled—you never know what might be hiding underground!
why_it_matters: Discovering treasures from the past reminds you that the ground beneath your feet might hold secrets, and that people long ago had skills and beliefs that still amaze us today.

background_read: Wat Thammachak Sema Ram is a Buddhist temple in central Thailand that houses the country's longest and oldest reclining Buddha statue, built in 657 A.D.
The Dvaravati period (which lasted from around the 6th to the 11th century) was a time when Indian-influenced art and religion flourished in what is now Thailand.
Phanombutr Chantrachot, the director-general of Thailand's Fine Arts Department, oversees the protection of such historic finds.
Article_Structure: WHO: Construction workers and Thailand's Fine Arts Department.
WHAT: Unearthed 33 ancient ornaments and three metal sheets decorated with Buddha images.
WHERE: At Wat Thammachak Sema Ram temple, beside a 1,300-year-old reclining Buddha.
WHY: The objects were likely ritual offerings buried to honor the Buddha statue, and discovering them helps historians understand ancient art and beliefs.

perspectives.description: Archaeologists and museum experts are delighted because these finds add to our knowledge of Dvaravati art and show how Buddhism and Hinduism mixed long ago.
Some people worry that construction work could accidentally damage undiscovered artifacts if careful oversight is not done.
Local people may feel proud that their temple holds such important treasures, which could attract visitors and help keep history alive.
